3. **1Sa 17:55 stands on the threshold of 18:1.** A formal oath by Saul's soul immediately precedes the knitting of Jonathan's soul to David's.
4. ◆ **The oath misused:** "**As the Lord lives**, I will run after him and get something from him" (Gehazi, 2Ki 5:20; §13.2).
- **God swears by his own soul:** "The Lord God has sworn by himself [*his nephesh*]" (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14; read in Batch D and E). The oath by a *nephesh* is used of God as well as of men.

- **The oath answers a claim of vengeance.** The murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. **The Lord has avenged** my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8). David: "As the Lord lives, **who has redeemed my life** out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). **The oath on David's own redeemed soul refuses a vengeance done on his behalf** (Batch H §1.4).

- **The oath formula frames the nearness of death.** "But truly, **as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death**" (1Sa 20:3). The oath by Jonathan's soul carries David's own peril.

- **A life pledged for a life.** Rahab asks: "swear to me by the Lord … **deliver our lives from death**" (Jos 2:12–13). The spies answer: "**Our life for yours even to death!**" (2:14). They do not swear by the Lord's life. **They pledge their own *nephesh***.

findings.text: What the sequences show [Claude reading]: The oath marks adherence at a cost.; Elisha's triple oath is the price of the double spirit.; The Shunammite uses Elisha's own oath against him. Her bitterness of soul becomes a hold on the prophet that he cannot refuse.; Uriah's oath by David's soul is kept against David's wish. The wine that should have lowered his guard fails (a failed threshold — Batch F §7). He dies for keeping it.; The oath by the soul can guard a life while refusing a life. Zedekiah swears secretly by "who made our souls" to spare Jeremiah's life. He then declines the life offered to him (38:17, 20), from fear (38:19). The oath and the refusal are in one conversation.; 1Sa 17:55 stands on the threshold of 18:1. A formal oath by Saul's soul immediately precedes the knitting of Jonathan's soul to David's.; The oath misused: "As the Lord lives, I will run after him and get something from him" (Gehazi, 2Ki 5:20; §13.2).; Revisit (Batch H): God swears by his own soul: "The Lord God has sworn by himself [*his nephesh*]" (Amo 6:8; Jer 51:14; read in Batch D and E). The oath by a *nephesh* is used of God as well as of men.; The oath answers a claim of vengeance. The murderers of Ish-bosheth: "your enemy, who sought your life. The Lord has avenged my lord the king" (2Sa 4:8). David: "As the Lord lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity" → he has them killed (4:9–12). The oath on David's own redeemed soul refuses a vengeance done on his behalf (Batch H §1.4).; Revisit (delta) — the oath with death in view: The oath formula frames the nearness of death. "But truly, as the Lord lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death" (1Sa 20:3). The oath by Jonathan's soul carries David's own peril.; A life pledged for a life. Rahab asks: "swear to me by the Lord … deliver our lives from death" (Jos 2:12–13). The spies answer: "Our life for yours even to death!" (2:14). They do not swear by the Lord's life. The questions come later, at Horeb ("What are you doing here?", 19:9).; This is the eating-and-drinking threshold of Batch F §7, reversed. There, the meal lowers the guard and something enters. The death-wish is almost always the soul's, in the *nephesh* idiom ("asked his soul to die"). The anguish is placed in the spirit and the bitterness in the soul (Job 7:11), and the life "lingers" after the will to live has gone (2Sa 1:9).

What answers the wish is seldom death. The answer is food (Elijah; Israel in Exo 16), a question (Jonah), or something to look at (Num 21).; It is granted only twice: to Samson, in one final act, and to Saul, by a hand that is then condemned.; To carry out another's death-wish is still to kill (2Sa 1:14–16).

findings.text: 16.3 The heart and soul measured against death: "I find something more bitter than death: the woman whose heart is snares and nets" (Ecc 7:26). The context is the searcher's own heart: "I turned my heart to know … the foolishness that is madness" (7:25).; [Claude reading] One heart searching finds another heart as the trap. The heart ready to die, and the hearts that weep (context Act 21:10–14): Agabus binds himself with Paul's belt: "Thus says the Holy Spirit …" (11); The disciples urge him not to go (12); "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die" (13); "since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, 'Let the will of the Lord be done'" (14); [Claude reading] The others' weeping breaks Paul's heart but does not bend it. Readiness to die and a broken heart sit together. The ending echoes Gethsemane ("your will be done", Mat 26:42; §7.3). Here the friends say it, not the one facing death.

"Flesh" meets death in three ways: as the cause, by orientation (Rom 7:5; 8:6, 13); as the place Christ entered in order to undo it (Heb 2:14); as the place where Jesus' life shows in the dying (2Co 4:11); This extends §7.2: the four circumstances of "flesh" each have a relation to death.

findings.text: Heb 2:15 names the inner effect of death as fear, and that fear as slavery.

The Spirit sets the term of Simeon's life (Luk 2:26). His release is peace (2:29). His next words move to Mary's soul pierced and "thoughts from many hearts" revealed (2:35). One scene holds Spirit, death, soul and heart.

M50 (the single non-M25 delta pair): "any participation in the Spirit, any affection [*splanchna*, bowels] and sympathy" (Phili 2:1) [D3]. Bowels are excluded as a study word (ruling 4). The pair is noted only: the Spirit is listed beside the visceral seat of compassion.

16.10 Life risked "to death" for others — the OT precedent: "Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death" (Judg 5:18). This is in the same song as "March on, my soul, with might!" (5:21; §3.2).; "Our life for yours even to death!" (Jos 2:14; §4 revisit); David "took his life in his hand" against the Philistine (1Sa 19:5); The men to David: "If half of us die, they will not care [*set heart*] about us. But you are worth ten thousand of us" (2Sa 18:3). The enemy's heart is indifferent to many deaths. One life is weighed at ten thousand.; "the men who were seeking your life are dead" (Exo 4:19) → Moses returns (4:20). The death of the hunters frees the hunted life.; "Why then are you laying a trap for my life to bring about my death?" (1Sa 28:9). This is the medium to the disguised Saul.; "we are about to bring great disaster upon ourselves [*our souls*]" (Jer 26:19). To put the prophet to death would harm the souls of those who kill him. It is set against Hezekiah, who "feared the Lord … and the Lord relented".; [Claude reading] Batch F §3.2 read "hating one's life" and "not loving one's life unto death" as NT discipleship. The OT already has the same shape in battle and in covenant pledges: the life risked "to the death" for a people, a household or a king. What the NT adds is the object, "for the name of the Lord Jesus" (Act 21:13), and the example, "poured out his soul to death" (Isa 53:12).

findings.text: 16.11 Before and after: death as the frame of a blessing, an evidence, a burial: "that my soul may bless you before I die" (Gen 27:4). The soul's blessing (§13.3) is framed by expected death. It is the last act of a dying soul, and it is taken by deceit.

Death as evidence that hardens: "not one of the livestock of Israel was dead. But the heart of Pharaoh was hardened" (Exo 9:7). The evidence is seen and the heart still hardens (§3.3). Evidence does not move the heart (compare Jacob, whose spirit revives on seeing, §2).
A dead man honoured for his grandfather's heart: Ahaziah "was put to death. They buried him, for they said, 'He is the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who sought the Lord with all his heart'" (2Ch 22:9)

16.11 Before and after: death as the frame of a blessing, an evidence, a burial: "let not my lord take it to heart" (2Sa 13:33; §16.6); "he who stays in this city shall die … he who goes out … shall have his life as a prize of war" (Jer 21:9; 38:2; §5.1)

"Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" (context Isa 22:12–14): "the Lord God of hosts called for weeping and mourning" (12); "and behold, joy and gladness, killing oxen … eating flesh and drinking wine" (13); "Surely this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die" (14); [Claude reading] The feast is held against a call to mourn, with death in view. The threshold (Batch F §7) is entered on purpose. What follows is the only verdict in the set that ties atonement to death itself.

findings.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: Life is held in the breath and the soul, and it is God's to give and gather.; "Living soul" is shared with the animals. God's breathing is what marks Gen 2:7.; One decision of God's heart could gather every breath back (Job 34:14–15).; In the flood narrative God's heart changes while man's heart does not (Gen 6:5–6 → 8:21).; *rûaḥ* moves across senses within a single passage, and the passage uses the movement: Eze 37: carrying Spirit → breath → winds → "my Spirit within you"; Judg 15: rushing Spirit → one's own spirit returning; Jon 4: an appointed wind that makes the soul wish to die; Strength and hardness are one word. *ḥāzaq* is courage, hardening and the nerve to kill, according to what the heart is set toward (§3.3). This mirrors the tender heart (Batch F §6): neither softness nor strength of heart has a fixed moral value.; Revisit (Batch H §7.4): more words of this kind — *nāṣar* (keep the heart / the "guarded" wily heart), *šāmar*, vengeance, fatness of soul and of heart, *šāgâ*, kinship-flesh.; The inner components give way in order. Samson (Judg 16): the soul vexed; the heart told; the strength gone; the Lord gone; The strength returns only when asked for, and joined to the soul's consent to die.; Jacob (Gen 45): heart numb → spirit revived by words and sight.; The soul is what one swears by and what one bargains for.; Oaths "as your soul lives" mark adherence at a cost (Elisha, the Shunammite, Uriah) or protection with fear (Zedekiah).; Souls are hunted for bread (Eze 13) and "captured" by the wise (Pro 11:30).; Nothing can be given in return for a soul (Mic 6:7–8; Mat 16:26).; Eating and drinking recur at inner thresholds, now in three registers: the merry heart (Batch F §7); the heart sustained by bread before it is made merry (Judg 19:5, 8); the soul that blesses after a meal and wine (Gen 27:25); Also: the sad heart at a feast that turns to prayer (Hannah, Nehemiah), and the wine-threshold refused (Uriah).; Enticement and stirring show how other agents reach the inner seat: God stirs human spirits (Cyrus, Pul, the remnant).; God sends an other-spirit to entice through prophets' mouths (1Ki 22).; God allures and speaks to the heart (Hos 2:14).; Desire, gods and false teachers entice hearts and souls.

findings.text: 14. Cross-cutting observations for Batch G [Claude reading]: The flesh is valued by circumstance: all living beings; mortal life lived by faith; Christ's own flesh; weakness; an orientation opposed to the Spirit. Joh 6 shifts its value within one discourse.; Life-hatred has two faces. The despairing soul of Job, Qohelet and Jonah hates life from exhaustion. The disciple hates it for another's sake (Batch F §3.2). The words overlap; the purpose differs.; Fringe worth keeping: the dead-but-assembled body without breath (Eze 37:8); Jacob's spirit reviving at the sight of wagons (Gen 45:27); Samson's two prayers (Judg 15:18; 16:28); Uriah's oath by the king's soul, kept against the king; the Shunammite turning Elisha's oath on him; Eli reading heart-prayer as drunkenness; "stumbling of heart" averted by Abigail; the lying spirit volunteering in the council; the idol told "Awake" with the verb that stirs Cyrus's spirit; Nebuchadnezzar's heart replaced by a beast's; Elisha's heart going out to meet Naaman's chariot; Isaac's soul blessing after wine; Revisit (delta) — the death side confirms and extends the life side: The inner seat can die before the body. Nabal's heart dies ten days before the Lord strikes him (§16.1).; At death the texts give each component its own verb. The soul "departs" (Rachel). The heart "does not attend" (Phinehas's wife). The spirit is "not retained" (Ecc 8:8) and is "gathered back" (Job 34:14).; *nephesh* names the corpse as well as the living creature (§16.7). What it names is the individual.; The death-wish belongs to the soul, and is seldom answered with death (§16.2, §6).; Food answers Elijah and the people. A question answers Jonah. Something to look at answers the people in Num 21.; It is granted to Samson in one last act. To Saul it is granted by a hand that is condemned for it.; Eating stands at the threshold between wanting to die and going on. This is the life-giving face of the eating threshold in Batch F §7.; The heart decides which death is just (§16.6, §5.4).; The law of refuge tests the killer's past hatred in the heart, and shields him from the avenger's hot heart.; Ransom is refused only for the life that took a life in hatred.; Where the law refuses a price, a mediator "finds a ransom" (Job 33:24). Love cannot be bought at all (Song 8:7).; Deliverance from death is for something (§16.4).
